Gastroenterology · published research

Colon anastomoses

Older rat studies reported greater early anastomotic strength and improved histology after low-dose red He-Ne laser. A higher fluence did not produce the same strength result, and human studies are absent.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Older rat studies reported greater early anastomotic strength and improved histology after low-dose red He-Ne laser. A higher fluence did not produce the same strength result, and human studies are absent.

Summary of the Evidence

Three publications from one Spanish research group examined low-power helium-neon laser after rat colon anastomosis. The 1988 and 1990 papers cover closely related early healing work, and possible overlap in experiments cannot be excluded. A 1992 paper tested high-risk anastomoses with a distinct dose comparison. They are three publications, but not clearly three independent research programmes. No human study or in-vitro/ex-vivo study was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

No clinical trial has shown that PBM reduces anastomotic leakage, infection, reoperation, or recovery time after human colorectal surgery. The animal measure of bursting strength is relevant to mechanical integrity but is not equivalent to clinical leak rates.

Animal evidence

In 1988, low-power He-Ne irradiation increased the bursting pressure and wall tension of rat colon anastomoses at postoperative days 2, 4, and 7, without the luminal narrowing seen in controls. In the related histology paper, two 3.6-J/cm² exposures increased fibroblasts and round cells in scar tissue, new-vessel formation, and epithelialization (Asencio-Arana et al. 1988; Asencio-Arana et al. 1990).

The 1992 high-risk model found that repeated 1.9-J/cm² exposure increased day-four bursting strength by nearly 100%. A higher 6.4-J/cm² dose did not show the same effect, and hydroxyproline differences were not statistically significant. This suggests a dose-specific result in that model rather than a general advantage from greater energy (Asencio-Arana et al. 1992).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No direct cell-culture or ex-vivo study of PBM for colon anastomosis was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The experiments used approximately 633-nm red visible He-Ne laser light. Reported fluences include 3.6 J/cm² in the early healing studies and 1.9 versus 6.4 J/cm² in the high-risk model. The 1992 treatment was applied endoscopically; other reports used local irradiation. The experiments did not compare modern devices or establish an optimal schedule. Rat tissue depth, surgical technique, and assessment over days differ from human postoperative care.

Interpretation

The papers consistently describe stronger early mechanical or histologic repair at selected low-energy protocols, and the 1992 dose comparison shows that the higher dose was not equally effective. This is a directional animal finding worth distinguishing from clinical proof. The reports are old, from one group, and do not show that PBM prevents leaks in patients.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for early anastomotic strength and healing measures in rats
Publications and records3 articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Three older rat publications report stronger early anastomoses or improved tissue repair after red He-Ne laser, but they come from one research group and possible cohort overlap is unresolved. The higher tested fluence did not reproduce the low-dose strength result. Independent modern animal studies and then surgical trials measuring leaks and complications would be needed to support a clinical claim.
